facts.claim: Anthropic bills the tokens Claude uses while thinking as output tokens, and bills the full thinking even when the response shows only a summary of it.
OpenAI’s reasoning tokens are not visible through the API, but they take up room in the context window and are billed as output tokens.
Anthropic’s effort setting takes the levels low, medium, high, xhigh and max (not every model offers all five); most models default to high.
Anthropic’s docs call effort a behavioural signal, not a strict token budget: at lower effort Claude still thinks on hard problems, but less than it would at higher effort.
With adaptive thinking, Claude weighs each request and decides whether to think and how much: a simple factual question may get no thinking at all, and a multistep problem gets deeper reasoning.
Anthropic’s fixed thinking budget (budget_tokens) is deprecated on the Claude 4.6 models and rejected by Claude 4.7 and later, which use adaptive thinking with an effort level instead.
OpenAI’s reasoning.effort takes values that depend on the model, from none and minimal through low, medium and high to xhigh and max; lower effort favours speed and fewer tokens.

Snell and colleagues (2024) found that how much extra thinking-time compute helps depends on how hard the question is, and that spending it well per question made it more than 4 times as efficient as a best-of-N baseline.

Gema and colleagues (2025) built tasks where longer reasoning makes large reasoning models less accurate, among them simple counting tasks with distractors: an inverse scaling between thinking-time compute and accuracy.
Anthropic’s docs advise testing each effort level on your own use cases before deploying, since its impact varies by task type.
